rationale: A wins because it keeps four real stories separated by protagonist and proof burden, especially "Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it," which has a grocer-side story hiding inside the announcement. B has useful bones, but "What 6,000 Consumer Brands Buying Grocery Ads Reveals About Where CPG Money Is Moving" is mostly the same ad-trade story in a new jacket, with an invented trend flourish about attribution. A also catches the landmine B keeps wandering near: the facts do not say carts are ad inventory.
gaps_in_A: "Instacart's delivery growth has stalled" overstates the supplied fact. The update says growth slowed to single digits; stalled means flat or near-flat.
"The checkout line is quietly disappearing from a few hundred grocery stores" is a touch grand. Caper carts skip checkout for their users; they do not prove checkout lines are disappearing storewide.

"1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack" is a useful retailer-strategy lens, but it needs care: the facts say Instacart partners with 1,500 banners, not that all are renting the same carts/e-commerce/ad stack.
gaps_in_B: "With $1B in Ad Revenue" is sloppy grounding. The fact is a $1B annual run rate, not necessarily recognized ad revenue.

"a stated plan to grow across 1,500+ banner partners" overclaims. The update says Instacart has 1,500+ retail-banner partners and plans to expand carts; it does not say the cart rollout is across all 1,500.
"as digital attribution has gotten harder" is an invented market peg. It may be true in the world, but it is not in the update and was not sourced.

The second and fourth angles are padded cousins: "retail media network" and "where CPG money is moving" both chase the same $1B/6,000-brand ad story without enough new evidence to justify two pitches.
